narration.text: A relationship between two entities is a familiar way of representing knowledge.
But even a simple sentence can describe something more complex. Michelangelo sent money to his brothers from Rome. Several participants belong to a single assertion.
We could represent this as several separate relationships. But how do we preserve the fact that they belong together?

caption: The relationships survive. Their grouping may not.

narration.text: Add another sending, involving a different object, recipient and place.
Without preserving the original grouping, we may no longer know which participants belong to which assertion.

caption: The statement becomes a first-class object.

narration.text: Instead, we can represent the assertion itself as an object: a Claim Statement.
Each participant connects to it through a particular semantic role.
Both statements describe sending, and both share a sender. Each retains its own identity.
An n-ary statement brings several participants together in one assertion.
And because the statement has its own identity, it can retain a connection to the passage from which it was derived.

caption: The assertion becomes an object of inquiry.

narration.text: The statement itself can now become something we identify, qualify, question and investigate.

caption: A statement is more than the sum of its relationships. Meaning is not always binary.

narration.text: A statement is more than the sum of its relationships.
